body_excerpt: ### Summary Add unit tests for `src.services.service_utils`, the shared utility module that powers sorting and search-filter translation across multiple v1 services. The module has two public helpers (`apply_sorting` and `_add_search_filters`) but has no direct test file — coverage is only incidental through integration tests. ## Background & Context `api/src/services/service_utils.py` exposes `apply_sorting(stmt, model, sort_order)` which translates sort orders into SQLAlchemy `asc()`/`desc()` calls. `_add_search_filters` maps the project's search filter types onto an OpenSearch query builder. The sorting helper is pure SQLAlchemy statement construction — no database required. The filter helper requires a mock `SearchQueryBuilder` but does not require running OpenSearch. Rule reference: `documentation/rules/api-services.md` ("Extract Shared Logic to Utility Files") and `documentation/rules/cross-domain.md` (CCP-3). ## Getting Started - File under test: `api/src/services/service_utils.py` - New test file: `api/tests/src/services/test_service_utils.py` - Types: `src.pagination.pagination_models.SortDirection`, `src.search.search_models.{Str,Bool,Int,Date}SearchFilter` - Local setup: `cd api && make format-check && make test` ## Technical Approach Source (`api/src/services/service_utils.py:15-78`): ```python def apply_sorting(stmt: Select, model: type, sort_order: list) -> Select: order_cols: list = [] for order in sort_order: column = getattr(model, order.order_by) if order.sort_direction == SortDirection.ASCENDING: order_cols.append(asc(column)) elif order.sort_direction == SortDirection.DESCENDING: order_cols.append(desc(column)) return stmt.order_by(*order_cols) ``` Use any existing model with a scalar column (e.g., `User.user_id`). For `_add_search_filters`, pass `Mock(spec=SearchQueryBuilder)` and assert on `mock.filter_terms.assert_called_once_with(...)`. ## Testing Requirements - Location: `api/tests/src/services/test_service_utils.py` - Tools: pytest, `unitt…

body_excerpt: ### **Description:** In 2026, agentic memory has a dirty secret: **your agent's memories are trapped.** Every memory platform stores your agent's accumulated knowledge — learned preferences, resolved contradictions, hard-won context — in its own proprietary schema. Switch tools, and it all evaporates. Your agent starts over with amnesia. We believe agentic memory should belong to *you*. That's why Memanto ships with a full migration and portability toolchain, built on the **[Open Knowledge Format (OKF)](https://docs.memanto.ai/integrations/okf)** — Google Cloud's open, vendor-neutral spec for knowledge as plain markdown. With Memanto today you can already: - **Migrate in** from Mem0, Letta, or Supermemory with a single command: [`memanto migrate`](https://docs.memanto.ai/cli/migrate/migrate) — complete with dry-run previews and token/latency/storage savings reports - **Export out** to a portable, git-friendly, human-readable OKF bundle: `memanto memory export --okf` - **Import any OKF bundle** losslessly: `memanto migrate okf ./bundle` — unmapped fields are preserved, nothing is lost - **Sync** a browsable memory wiki into any project: `memanto memory sync --okf` The tools exist. What the world hasn't seen yet is the **movement**. We want the open-source community to show every agent builder — vividly, virally, with real data — what it looks like to *escape lock-in and own your memory*. ### **The Challenge:** Build a **compelling, reproducible migration showcase** that takes memories from another tool into Memanto and out again as portable OKF — proving the full freedom loop: **in → owned → portable**. ⚠️ **Do NOT reinvent the wheel.** The `memanto migrate` CLI and OKF export/import are shipped and documented. Your job is to build *on top of* them — real-world showcases, new migration paths for tools we don't support yet, and creative OKF workflows. Submissions that re-implement what the CLI already does will score poorly on engineering value. ### 💡 Pick Your Path…

body_excerpt: ## Description: In a previous bounty, we asked the community to stress-test **Memanto** in order to find bugs, logic loops, and performance bottlenecks. We got an unexpectedly large number of PR's and we’ve spent a great deal of time meticulously reviewing them, you’ve all helped us make a huge step forward in improving the security and quality of Memanto! Now, we are taking it a step further and focusing exclusively on what matters most for AI in production: **Security**. As memory layers become the backbone of autonomous agents, they also become a prime target for attacks. Whether it's a cross-tenant data leak, a broken access control, or a malicious payload hidden in a retrieved memory, we want to know about it. We’ve fixed a majority of bugs and issues with Memanto and resolved many of its security issues, but as Memanto starts to be utilized in more sensitive workflows, we want to ensure our defenses are as robust as possible and we need the developer community to help us do that. Your mission is simple: **Help us audit our memory management and backend infrastructure to uncover potential vulnerabilities before they can be exploited.** --- ## 🎯 Threat Model & Scope Your target is the `memanto` core package and its interaction with the `moorcheh.ai` serverless backend.
